newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian firms seen weaker, then many picking up.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian firms seen weaker, then many picking up.

text.p: Hungarian firms are expected to release weaker third quarter results but many may recoup in the last three months of the year, analysts said.

"It's possible that the third quarter will not be strong for many companies but in the last quarter of the year many industries can compensate for this," said Gabor Sitanyi, London-based analyst for ING Barings.
Companies in the listed A category of the Budapest Stock Exchange, one of the world's fastest growing bourses, have to submit their January-September reports by November 15.
The analysts were divided over the possible impact of the results on share prices on the Budapest bourse whose BUX share index has more than doubled this year.
With a public holiday on Wednesday, Tuesday saw the BUX index close at 3,615.75 points, below the all-time record high of 3,728.58 points reached on October 17.

"The results will hardly cause any positive or negative surprises because investors are aware of (industries') seasonality," Sitanyi said. "Expectations for the third quarter are beginning to be reflected in share prices so I don't expect the results in themselves to move the market."
But Tibor Papp, sales executive in Budapest at Raiffeisen Securities, was more optimistic.
"These companies enjoy quite a good international assessment," Papp said. "Unless the assessment changes...the market may continue to firm after the current falls."
The energy, chemical and pharmaceutical companies were regarded as the most affected by seasonal factors.
"The pharmaceuticals' third quarter is generally weaker because price increases occur in the first quarter and wholesalers make stock-piling ahead of the rises," Sitanyi said.
Chemicals makers Borsodchem and TVK were also seen hit by relatively low international PVC prices, although these have risen since mid-September.
Oil and gas company MOL was also seen as having potential problems ahead.

"(In the third quarter) gas consumption declines, while oil prices went up a lot and MOL is a net importer, so refinery margins may have narrowed," Spencer Jakab, Budapest-based analyst at CS First Boston, said.
The key question for MOL is the size of energy price rise which was postponed to January 1, 1997 from October 1996.
The government has not made any proposals yet although Prime Minister Gyula Horn earlier this month said that he could envisage a 23 percent increase.
However, analysts are mostly bullish regarding the building sector.
"I expect strong figures from construction companies, mainly from (tile manufacturer) Zalakeramia and (plastics industrial) Pannonplast," Jakab said.

Zalakeramia, he said, has additional capacity already operational in the third quarter in its new Romhany unit, while Pannonplast's diversified product range protects it from sharp price fluctuations.
The banking sector seems to be the least influenced by seasonal factors.
"The only factor which can cause seasonality is if the banks' provisions are not made on schedule or if some cost items are booked only in the fourth quarter," Sitanyi said.
